p.x:
This year, my friend Fah became our class president. Everyone voted, and she was the winner! She is also the team leader of our science group.
Fah is a good leader. When we can't decide what to do, she listens to everyone. She always encourages people who are shy. Our teacher says she might become head girl one day. The head boy this year is in Grade 12.
Last month, Fah organised a school clean-up day. Even the chief of the local council came to help! I'm proud of my friend.

Leaders are everywhere: the CEO of a company, the captain of a sports team, or a prefect at school. But what makes someone a good leader?
First, a leader needs a vision, a clear idea of where the group is going. Then they must make decisions, sometimes very difficult ones. A good leader is organised and trustworthy, and people feel they can depend on them. An inspiring leader makes others want to work hard.
Good leaders don't just give orders. They lead by example, doing the same hard work they ask others to do. They are approachable, so team members feel comfortable sharing ideas. When things go wrong, they admit their mistakes instead of blaming others, and they never take credit for someone else's work.
In a crisis, leaders must be decisive and stay calm under pressure. When someone else is not there, a good leader is ready to take charge. Some leaders use a democratic style, asking the group to reach a consensus. Others prefer to decide alone. A leader who is a team player usually earns more respect. A persuasive leader can convince people to follow a new idea. Finally, a wise leader knows when it is time to step down and let someone else lead.

For much of history, leadership was associated with power and control. The traditional model was top-down: decisions were made by a small group at the top and passed down to workers who were expected to obey. Authoritarian leaders, whether in politics or business, demanded loyalty and rarely tolerated disagreement.
In recent decades, ideas about leadership have changed considerably. Researchers have found that emotional intelligence, the ability to understand and manage one's own emotions and those of others, is often more important than technical expertise. The concept of servant leadership suggests that a leader's primary role is to support and develop their team rather than to command it.
Charisma remains a powerful quality, and history is full of visionary leaders whose ideas transformed societies. However, charisma alone can be dangerous if it is not accompanied by honesty and good judgement. Many organisations now value pragmatic leaders who focus on practical solutions rather than grand promises.
Questions of diversity are also central to modern discussions of leadership. Women remain under-represented in senior positions in many countries, held back by what has been called the glass ceiling. Companies with diverse leadership teams, studies suggest, often make better decisions. Choosing a successor is one of a leader's most important responsibilities; in some organisations, a chairperson may remain merely a figurehead while others are at the helm, making the real decisions.
